title: Establish SDK request taxonomy and triage rules for language gaps, auth patterns, and streaming ergonomics
creator: Aisha Khan
description: Objective: Create a clear, operational taxonomy and a weighted triage rubric for SDK and client-library feature requests coming from customers and solutions engineering. Scope covers three high-frequency request categories: 1) language bindings and packaging gaps (new languages, platform-specific packaging, native mobile bindings), 2) authentication and token lifecycle patterns (SSO/SAML, service accounts, token rotation, KMS integration), and 3) streaming ergonomics and backpressure semantics (client-side buffering, reconnect/backoff strategies, server streaming vs chunked responses).
acceptance_criteria: 1) A one-page taxonomy doc that maps inbound request types to canonical outcomes (Accept for roadmap / Defer to polyglot layer / Redirect to best-effort SDK adapter / Close as duplicate). 2) A scoring rubric with numeric weights for security exposure, enterprise impact, estimated engineering effort, risk to backward compatibility, and revenue signal. 3) A recommended operational flow: intake form fields, automatic labels, required reviewers (Security/SE/Design), and SLA for initial response. 4) Sample decisions for five representative requests (Go mobile bindings, token rotation SDK helper, streaming reconnect semantics, Node small-bundle variant, OAuth service account onboarding).
notes_summary: Motivation: increased volume of customer asks with inconsistent ask detail and duplicated tickets across languages; Sales and Solutions Eng ask for predictable timelines for enterprise onboarding. Constraints: limited eng bandwidth, desire to keep core SDK API stable, security/compliance requirements for enterprise features. Trade-offs: build many idiomatic language libs (higher short-term dev cost) vs ship lightweight cross-language adapters (lower cost, higher client friction). Proposed middle-ground: prioritize deep support for languages with high production adoption (Python, JS/Node, Java, Go, Kotlin/Swift for mobile) and offer official lightweight adapters and reference implementations for others.
